levels.name: Beginner
levels.desc: Your first steps: the alphabet, greetings, basic sentence structure, the present tense, and the core building blocks that every later level depends on.
levels.goal: introduce yourself, order food, ask simple questions, and handle everyday situations

topics.summary: German uses the same 26 letters as English, plus four extra characters: three umlauts (ä ö ü) and the sharp S (ß). Spelling is far more consistent than English — once you learn the sound rules below, you can read almost any German word correctly on sight.

cards.desc: ä ≈ “e” in “bed”, ö ≈ French “eu”, ü ≈ French “u” / a tight “ee”. When typing without umlauts, write ae, oe, ue instead.
Straße (street) sounds like “SHTRAH-suh”. Switzerland writes “ss” instead of ß — both are correct.

cards.de: W = English V, V = English F
cards.desc: Wasser sounds like “Vasser”. Vater sounds like “Fater”. This trips up almost every beginner.
After i/e (ich) it's a soft hiss at the front of the mouth. After a/o/u (Buch) it's a hard rasp from the throat.

topics.rule_note: Every German noun is capitalised, and almost every letter is pronounced — there are no silent letters like the “k” in “knife”. If you can spell it, you can say it.
topics.table_sub: The sounds that differ most from English

example_main.de: Schönen guten Morgen, wie geht es Ihnen?
example_main.en: Good morning, how are you? (formal)

extra_examples.de: Ich heiße Mustafa und komme aus dem Irak.
extra_examples.en: My name is Mustafa and I come from Iraq.

extra_examples.de: Die Straße ist sehr groß.
extra_examples.en: The street is very big.

extra_examples.de: Wir hören zusammen deutsche Musik.
extra_examples.en: We listen to German music together.

extra_examples.de: Vier Freunde fahren nach Würzburg.
extra_examples.en: Four friends are traveling to Würzburg.

topics.tip: Say the alphabet out loud once a day for a week using the sounds above — German spelling is so regular that solid letter-sound instincts will let you read new words correctly on your first try.
topics.warning: Don’t read v and w the English way — “Wasser” is not “Wasser” as an English speaker would say it, it’s “Vasser”. This single habit affects hundreds of common words.

quick_check.q: How do you type ü without an umlaut key?

topics.summary: German has a formal and an informal “you” (Sie vs. du), and the right greeting depends on the time of day. Master this set of fixed phrases first — they cover a huge share of daily small talk.

cards.desc: Use Sie with strangers, officials, and at work until invited otherwise. Use du with friends, family, children, and (usually) colleagues your own age.
Guten Morgen (until ~10 am) → Guten Tag (daytime) → Guten Abend (evening). “Hallo” and “Servus” (south) work any time, informally.
Like “How are you” in English, Germans usually answer briefly: “Gut, danke, und dir/Ihnen?”, even if the day was average.
“Auf Wiedersehen” is formal/neutral. “Tschüss” and “Bis bald” are informal. “Gute Nacht” is only for going to bed.

topics.rule_note: Introduce yourself with Ich heiße… (My name is…) or Ich bin… (I am…) — both are correct and used interchangeably in everyday speech.
topics.table_sub: Learn these as whole chunks, not word-by-word
table_rows: Wie heißen Sie? / Wie heißt du?

example_main.de: Guten Tag, ich heiße Mustafa. Freut mich, Sie kennenzulernen.
example_main.en: Hello, my name is Mustafa. Pleased to meet you.

extra_examples.de: Hallo Anna, wie geht’s dir?
extra_examples.en: Hi Anna, how are you?

extra_examples.de: Guten Abend, Herr Schmidt. Wie geht es Ihnen?
extra_examples.en: Good evening, Mr Schmidt. How are you?

extra_examples.de: Danke, mir geht es sehr gut. Und Ihnen?
extra_examples.en: Thanks, I’m doing very well. And you?

extra_examples.de: Entschuldigung, wo ist der Bahnhof?
extra_examples.en: Excuse me, where is the train station?

extra_examples.de: Es war schön, dich zu treffen. Bis bald!
extra_examples.en: It was nice to meet you. See you soon!

topics.tip: In job interviews and with anyone older or senior to you, default to Sie — it’s never rude to be too formal, but switching to du too early can sound presumptuous.

quick_check.q: Which greeting is used only in the evening?

topics.summary: “sein” (to be) and “haben” (to have) are the two most important verbs in German — both are irregular, both are used constantly, and both are the building blocks of the past tense you’ll learn in A2. Memorise these two conjugations before anything else.

cards.desc: ich (I), du (you, informal), er/sie/es (he/she/it). German “it” also applies to nouns — der/die/das all become er/sie/es.
wir (we), ihr (you-all, informal plural), sie (they), Sie (you, formal — always capitalised, singular or plural).
Used for identity, nationality, profession, feelings: Ich bin Müde (I am tired).
Used for possession, age, and many fixed expressions: Ich habe Hunger (lit. “I have hunger” = I’m hungry).

topics.rule_note: German verbs change their ending for every pronoun (this is called conjugation). Because the verb ending already shows who’s doing the action, native speakers sometimes drop the pronoun in casual speech — but as a learner, always include it.
topics.table_sub: The two verbs you will use every single day

example_main.de: Ich bin Netzwerktechniker und habe viel Erfahrung.
example_main.en: I am a network technician and have a lot of experience.

extra_examples.de: Wir sind müde, aber wir haben noch Zeit.
extra_examples.en: We are tired, but we still have time.

extra_examples.de: Bist du bereit? Hast du deinen Pass?
extra_examples.en: Are you ready? Do you have your passport?

extra_examples.de: Sie ist Ingenieurin und hat zwei Kinder.
extra_examples.en: She is an engineer and has two children.

extra_examples.de: Habt ihr Hunger? Seid ihr auch durstig?
extra_examples.en: Are you (all) hungry? Are you thirsty too?

topics.warning: Don’t translate “I am 30 years old” with sein — German uses haben: Ich habe 30 Jahre is wrong; the fixed idiom is Ich bin 30 Jahre alt (with sein + alt). But hunger, thirst, and fear DO use haben: Ich habe Hunger/Durst/Angst.

topics.summary: Every German noun has a grammatical gender — masculine, feminine, or neuter — shown by its article (der/die/das). Gender is not always logical (das Mädchen, “the girl”, is neuter), so the safest strategy is to learn every new noun together with its article, as one unit.

cards.desc: Many job titles for men, days, months, and seasons are masculine: der Lehrer, der Montag, der Winter.
Most nouns ending in -e, -ung, -heit, -keit, -ion, -tion are feminine: die Zeitung, die Freiheit, die Information.
Diminutives (-chen, -lein) and most nouns borrowed from English are neuter: das Mädchen, das Handy, das Internet.
In the plural, gender disappears — der/die/das ALL become die: die Männer, die Frauen, die Kinder.

topics.rule_note: Learn der Tisch, not just Tisch — the article is part of the word’s identity and you will need it constantly for cases (Unit 8) and adjective endings later on.
topics.table_title: Gender Patterns You Can Rely On
topics.table_sub: Not perfect rules, but strong tendencies

example_main.de: Der Tisch, die Lampe und das Fenster sind neu.
example_main.en: The table, the lamp, and the window are new.

extra_examples.de: Die Wohnung hat ein großes Fenster.
extra_examples.en: The apartment has a big window.

extra_examples.de: Das Handy liegt auf dem Tisch.
extra_examples.en: The phone is lying on the table.

extra_examples.de: Der Computer und die Tastatur sind kaputt.
extra_examples.en: The computer and the keyboard are broken.

extra_examples.de: Die Männer und die Frauen arbeiten zusammen.
extra_examples.en: The men and the women work together.

topics.tip: Colour-code your vocabulary notes: blue for der, red for die, green for das. Visual memory sticks far better than a plain word list for something as arbitrary as grammatical gender.
topics.warning: das Mädchen (the girl) is grammatically neuter, not feminine — because it ends in -chen. Grammatical gender is not the same as biological sex; don’t try to guess by meaning alone.

quick_check.q: What’s the plural article for ALL nouns?

topics.summary: English mostly just adds “-s”. German has five different plural patterns, and the correct one depends on the word — sometimes with an added umlaut. There’s no single rule, so plurals are learned noun-by-noun, but a few strong tendencies will get you very far.

cards.desc: Very common for masculine nouns: der Hund → die Hunde. With umlaut: der Stuhl → die Stühle.
Common for short neuter nouns: das Buch → die Bücher, das Haus → die Häuser.
Almost all feminine nouns take -n or -en, and NEVER add an umlaut: die Lampe → die Lampen.
Words borrowed from other languages usually just add -s, like in English: das Hotel → die Hotels.

topics.rule_note: There is a fifth, “invisible” pattern too: some masculine and neuter nouns don’t change at all — only the article shifts to die: der Lehrer → die Lehrer, das Zimmer → die Zimmer.
topics.table_sub: Learn the pattern, not just the word

example_main.de: Ich habe drei Bücher und zwei Hefte in meiner Tasche.
example_main.en: I have three books and two notebooks in my bag.

extra_examples.de: Die Kinder spielen mit den Hunden im Park.
extra_examples.en: The children are playing with the dogs in the park.

extra_examples.de: Wir haben viele Freunde in Deutschland.
extra_examples.en: We have many friends in Germany.

extra_examples.de: Die Häuser in dieser Straße sind sehr alt.
extra_examples.en: The houses on this street are very old.

extra_examples.de: Meine Kollegen benutzen neue Computer.
extra_examples.en: My colleagues are using new computers.

topics.tip: Whenever you learn a new noun, learn it in a three-part chunk: article + singular + plural, e.g. “das Buch, die Bücher”. Good dictionaries and apps always show the plural for exactly this reason.

quick_check.q: Do feminine nouns ever add an umlaut in the plural?

topics.summary: German marks the role of a noun in a sentence with “case” endings on the article, not with word order like English. The nominative marks the subject (who does the action); the accusative marks the direct object (who/what receives it). Only the masculine article actually changes between the two.

cards.desc: Der Mann sieht den Hund. — “Der Mann” is the subject: he is doing the seeing.

cards.en: Who or what is acted on
cards.desc: Der Mann sieht den Hund. — “den Hund” receives the action: he is being seen.
Feminine (die), neuter (das) and plural (die) articles stay IDENTICAL in nominative and accusative.
The indefinite article follows the same rule: ein Mann (subject) → einen Mann (object) — masculine only.

topics.rule_note: Ask yourself “who/what is doing this?” for nominative, and “who/what is receiving this?” for accusative. In Ich sehe den Hund (I see the dog), “Ich” is nominative and “den Hund” is accusative.

example_main.de: Der Kunde kauft einen Laptop und eine Maus.
example_main.en: The customer is buying a laptop and a mouse.

extra_examples.de: Ich brauche einen neuen Router für das Büro.
extra_examples.en: I need a new router for the office.

extra_examples.de: Die Firma sucht einen Netzwerktechniker.
extra_examples.en: The company is looking for a network technician.

extra_examples.de: Kennst du den Mann dort? — Ja, das ist mein Kollege.
extra_examples.en: Do you know that man over there? — Yes, that’s my colleague.

extra_examples.de: Wir haben das Problem schnell gelöst.
extra_examples.en: We solved the problem quickly.

topics.warning: Certain prepositions ALWAYS take the accusative, whatever they attach to — memorise them as a set: für, durch, gegen, ohne, um (for, through, against, without, around). “für den Kunden” (for the customer) is always accusative, never dative.

quick_check.q: Which article never changes between nominative and accusative?

topics.summary: Most German verbs are “regular” (weak) and follow one predictable pattern: strip “-en” off the infinitive to get the stem, then add the ending that matches the subject. Master this one pattern and you can conjugate hundreds of verbs correctly on your first try.

cards.desc: Take any infinitive (the dictionary form, always ending in -en or -n) and remove that ending to get the stem.
ich spiele, du spielst, er spielt, wir spielen, ihr spielt, sie spielen.
An extra -e- is inserted before -st/-t for easier pronunciation: du arbeitest, er arbeitet (not “arbeitst”).
du + stem already ending in an s-sound drops the extra s: du heißt (not “heißst”), du tanzt (not “tanzst”).

topics.rule_note: German has only one present tense where English has two: “ich spiele” covers both “I play” and “I am playing”. There is no separate “be + -ing” form to learn.
topics.table_sub: The pattern that fits most German verbs

example_main.de: Ich arbeite in einem Rechenzentrum und lerne jeden Tag Deutsch.
example_main.en: I work in a data center and learn German every day.

extra_examples.de: Sie wohnt in Bagdad und lernt Deutsch am Abend.
extra_examples.en: She lives in Baghdad and learns German in the evening.

extra_examples.de: Wir kaufen Brot und Milch im Supermarkt.
extra_examples.en: We buy bread and milk at the supermarket.

extra_examples.de: Machst du heute Abend noch etwas?
extra_examples.en: Are you doing anything else tonight?

extra_examples.de: Die Kollegen arbeiten bis achtzehn Uhr.
extra_examples.en: The colleagues work until six p.m.

topics.tip: Once “-en” verbs feel automatic, notice how few truly irregular verbs there are (Unit 10 and this unit’s warning box) — German rewards you for learning the regular pattern first.
topics.warning: A handful of very common verbs change their stem vowel for du and er/sie/es only: fahren → du fährst, er fährt; sprechen → du sprichst, er spricht; lesen → du liest, er liest. The endings stay the same — only the vowel shifts.

quick_check.q: Why does “du heißst” not become “du heißst-st”?
quick_check.a: the stem already ends in an s-sound, so no extra -st is added

topics.summary: Modal verbs express ability, permission, necessity or desire, and always push the main verb to the very end of the sentence in its infinitive form. They are irregular but only six words — learn them once and unlock an enormous range of everyday expression.

cards.de: können — can / to be able to
cards.desc: Ability or possibility: I can speak German.
Necessity or obligation: I have to go now.

cards.de: dürfen — may / to be allowed to
cards.desc: Permission (or its absence): You’re not allowed to smoke here.

cards.de: wollen / möchten — want to / would like to
cards.desc: wollen = strong will; möchten = polite “would like”. Always prefer möchten when ordering or requesting.

topics.rule_note: Verb-second, infinitive-last: the modal verb takes the normal 2nd-position verb slot and conjugates; the main verb goes to the very end, unconjugated: “Ich kann gut Deutsch sprechen.” This “verb bracket” (Satzklammer) is one of the defining features of German.
stats: Endings on the pushed-back main verb
topics.table_title: The Six Modal Verbs — Present Tense
topics.table_sub: ich/er forms are irregular — no ending at all

example_main.de: Ich muss heute länger arbeiten, aber ich kann morgen früh gehen.
example_main.en: I have to work longer today, but I can leave early tomorrow.

extra_examples.de: Kannst du mir bitte helfen?
extra_examples.en: Can you help me, please?

extra_examples.de: Wir möchten einen Tisch für zwei Personen.
extra_examples.en: We would like a table for two people.

extra_examples.de: Man darf hier nicht parken.
extra_examples.en: You’re not allowed to park here.

extra_examples.de: Ich will in Deutschland arbeiten und muss deshalb Deutsch lernen.
extra_examples.en: I want to work in Germany, so I have to learn German.

topics.tip: “Möchten” (would like) is technically the Konjunktiv II form of “mögen” (to like), but every learner uses it constantly from day one — it’s the politest way to order, ask, or request anything.

quick_check.q: Where does the main verb go with a modal verb?
quick_check.a: to the very end of the sentence, unconjugated

topics.summary: German has exactly two question patterns. W-questions start with a question word and ask for new information. Yes/No questions have no question word and simply flip the verb to the front of the sentence. Both always put the conjugated verb in second position or first — never buried in the middle like a statement.

cards.desc: Wer ist das? (Who is that?) Was machst du? (What are you doing?) Wo wohnst du? (Where do you live?)
Wann kommst du? (When are you coming?) Wie heißt du? (What’s your name?) Warum lernst du Deutsch? (Why are you learning German?)
Wie viel kostet das? (How much does that cost?) Wie viele Kinder hast du? (How many children do you have?)
Statement: Du sprichst Deutsch. → Question: Sprichst du Deutsch? — the verb simply moves to position 1.

topics.rule_note: In a W-question the order is: question word → verb → subject → rest. “Wo wohnst du?” — the verb is always the second element, right after the question word.
topics.table_sub: Memorise this set — it’s used in every conversation

example_main.de: Wo arbeitest du, und wie lange schon?
example_main.en: Where do you work, and for how long already?

extra_examples.de: Sprichst du auch Englisch?
extra_examples.en: Do you also speak English?

extra_examples.de: Hast du morgen Zeit?
extra_examples.en: Do you have time tomorrow?

extra_examples.de: Warum möchtest du in Deutschland arbeiten?
extra_examples.en: Why would you like to work in Germany?

extra_examples.de: Woher kommst du und wohin fliegst du?
extra_examples.en: Where are you from and where are you flying to?

topics.tip: German doesn’t use a helper word like “do/does” for yes/no questions the way English does — just move the conjugated verb to the front: “Learnst du Deutsch?” becomes simply “Lernst du Deutsch?”

quick_check.q: Turn “Du wohnst hier” into a yes/no question
Which W-word asks about a reason?

topics.summary: German has two negation words where English just has “not/no”. Choosing the right one depends on what you’re negating: a whole verb/adjective (nicht) or a noun that had “ein/eine” or no article (kein). Mixing them up is one of the most common beginner mistakes — and one of the easiest to fix.

cards.desc: Replaces ein/eine or an article-less noun: Ich habe einen Hund. → Ich habe keinen Hund.
Das ist nicht richtig. (That’s not correct.) Ich arbeite heute nicht. (I’m not working today.)

cards.de: nicht usually goes near the end
cards.desc: It sits right before the part being negated — often just before the verb-final infinitive/adjective: Ich kann heute nicht kommen.
kein follows the exact same ending pattern as ein/eine across all four cases — what you learn for “ein” transfers directly.

topics.rule_note: Quick test: can you insert “a/an” or “some” before the English noun? If yes, use kein. Everything else (verbs, adjectives, already-defined “the” nouns) uses nicht.

rules_table.title: nicht vs. kein — Side by Side
rules_table.sub: The same idea, negated two different ways

example_main.de: Ich habe heute keine Zeit, aber ich vergesse dich nicht.
example_main.en: I don’t have time today, but I won’t forget you.

extra_examples.de: Das ist kein gutes Angebot.
extra_examples.en: That’s not a good offer.

extra_examples.de: Wir arbeiten am Sonntag nicht.
extra_examples.en: We don’t work on Sundays.

extra_examples.de: Er hat keinen Führerschein.
extra_examples.en: He doesn’t have a driver’s licence.

extra_examples.de: Das Meeting ist heute nicht, sondern morgen.
extra_examples.en: The meeting isn’t today, but tomorrow.

topics.warning: Don’t say “Ich habe nicht ein Auto” — a native speaker will always say „Ich habe kein Auto.“ Using nicht to negate a noun with “ein” is the single most common negation mistake.

topics.summary: Family vocabulary is some of the highest-value vocabulary you can learn — it comes up constantly in small talk. Alongside it, you’ll meet possessive articles (mein, dein…) in the nominative case; you’ll see their full case endings in A2.

cards.desc: mein Vater (my father), meine Mutter (my mother) — the ending matches the noun’s gender, just like “ein”.
sein Bruder (his brother), ihre Schwester (her sister) — “ihr” is also “your (pl.)”, context tells them apart.
unser Haus (our house), euer Auto (your(pl.) car), Ihr Name (your name — formal, capitalised).
die Eltern (parents), die Geschwister (siblings) — always plural, even for one sibling context.

topics.rule_note: Possessive articles decline exactly like ein: mein/meine/mein in the nominative (masc./fem./neut.), and mein → meinen in the accusative masculine — same pattern as Unit 6.
topics.table_sub: der/die/das given for every noun

example_main.de: Meine Familie ist groß: Ich habe zwei Brüder und eine Schwester.
example_main.en: My family is big: I have two brothers and one sister.

extra_examples.de: Mein Vater arbeitet als Ingenieur, meine Mutter zu Hause.
extra_examples.en: My father works as an engineer, my mother at home.

extra_examples.de: Ist das deine Schwester? — Nein, das ist meine Kollegin.
extra_examples.en: Is that your sister? — No, that’s my colleague.

extra_examples.de: Unsere Eltern wohnen nicht in dieser Stadt.
extra_examples.en: Our parents don’t live in this city.

extra_examples.de: Wie heißt eure Mutter?
extra_examples.en: What’s your (pl.) mother’s name?

topics.tip: “Geschwister” has no natural English equivalent — it means “siblings” and is used even if someone has only one brother or sister. “Ich habe eine Schwester” is more natural than “Ich habe ein Geschwister”.

topics.summary: Telling the time, naming the days and months, and describing the seasons are essential survival skills — and they show up on forms, in scheduling emails, and in every calendar invite you’ll receive at a German company.

cards.desc: Montag, Dienstag, Mittwoch, Donnerstag, Freitag, Samstag, Sonntag — all masculine (der), never capitalised mid-sentence differently from other nouns.
der Frühling (spring), der Sommer (summer), der Herbst (autumn), der Winter (winter) — all masculine.
18:00 Uhr = 6 p.m. Spoken casual German still uses 12-hour time with “morgens/abends” added for clarity.
“halb acht” literally means “halfway to eight” — it’s 7:30, the opposite of the English instinct.

topics.rule_note: For “on [day]” German uses am: am Montag (on Monday). For “in [month]” it uses im: im Januar (in January). Both are fixed contractions (an+dem, in+dem) you just memorise.
topics.table_sub: Clock phrases you’ll use every day

example_main.de: Das Meeting ist am Montag um halb neun.
example_main.en: The meeting is on Monday at 8:30.

extra_examples.de: Im Winter arbeite ich oft von zu Hause.
extra_examples.en: In winter I often work from home.

extra_examples.de: Wir haben im Juli Urlaub.
extra_examples.en: We have vacation in July.

extra_examples.de: Der Zug fährt um Viertel vor sieben.
extra_examples.en: The train leaves at quarter to seven.

extra_examples.de: Am Wochenende habe ich frei.
extra_examples.en: I’m off on the weekend.

topics.warning: “halb acht” is 7:30, not 8:30 — this is the single most common time-telling mistake for English and Arabic speakers. Think “halfway TO eight”, not “half PAST eight”.

topics.summary: Ordinal numbers (first, second, third…) are used constantly for dates, floors, and rankings. German builds them with a simple suffix rule almost identical to the pattern you already saw for numbers — and dates always follow a strict day-month-year order.

cards.desc: vier → der vierte (4th). Two exceptions: erste (1st) and dritte (3rd) are irregular.
From 20 onward, the ending switches to -ste: der zwanzigste (20th), der einunddreißigste (31st).
“On the 10th of May” = am zehnten Mai — the ordinal takes a dative -n ending after “am”.
Germany writes dates day-month-year with full stops, never month-first like the US format.

topics.rule_note: Say your birthday as: Ich bin am + [ordinal]+n + [Monat] geboren — „Ich bin am zehnten Mai geboren.“ (I was born on the 10th of May.)
topics.table_sub: Watch the two irregular forms in bold

example_main.de: Mein Vertrag beginnt am ersten März.
example_main.en: My contract starts on the 1st of March.

extra_examples.de: Heute ist der fünfzehnte September.
extra_examples.en: Today is the 15th of September.

extra_examples.de: Ich habe am dritten Oktober Geburtstag.
extra_examples.en: My birthday is on the 3rd of October.

extra_examples.de: Das Meeting ist am zweiundzwanzigsten Januar.
extra_examples.en: The meeting is on the 22nd of January.

extra_examples.de: Wir ziehen am ersten Juli um.
extra_examples.en: We’re moving on the 1st of July.

topics.tip: Fill out German forms (Anmeldung, contracts, etc.) with the date as DD.MM.YYYY — writing it the US way (MM.DD.YYYY) is a common and confusing mistake for newcomers.

quick_check.q: How do you say “8th” in German?

topics.summary: Colors and everyday descriptive adjectives round out your ability to describe the world around you. Used after “sein” (predicative position), adjectives stay in their plain dictionary form and need no ending at all — a welcome piece of simplicity before adjective endings return in A2/B1.

cards.desc: rot (red), blau (blue), grün (green), gelb (yellow), schwarz (black), weiß (white), grau (grey), braun (brown).
After sein/werden, adjectives never change: Das Auto ist rot. Die Jacke ist schwarz.
Before a noun, adjectives DO take an ending (full rules in B1) — for now, just recognise the pattern.
groß/klein (big/small), neu/alt (new/old), teuer/billig (expensive/cheap), gut/schlecht (good/bad).

topics.rule_note: For now, remember the simple version: adjective after “sein” = no ending. “Der Pullover ist grün” needs no change — you’ll learn the “der grüne Pullover” pattern later.
topics.table_sub: Practical shopping and describing vocabulary

example_main.de: Ich suche eine schwarze Hose und ein weißes Hemd.
example_main.en: I’m looking for black trousers and a white shirt.

extra_examples.de: Diese Jacke ist zu teuer, haben Sie etwas Billigeres?
extra_examples.en: This jacket is too expensive, do you have something cheaper?

extra_examples.de: Der blaue Pullover gefällt mir sehr.
extra_examples.en: I like the blue sweater a lot.

extra_examples.de: Meine Schuhe sind alt, ich brauche neue.
extra_examples.en: My shoes are old, I need new ones.

extra_examples.de: Welche Farbe hat dein neues Auto? — Es ist grau.
extra_examples.en: What color is your new car? — It’s grey.

topics.tip: “Welche Farbe” (“which color”) rather than “was für eine Farbe” is the natural way to ask about color in everyday speech — keep the phrase “Welche Farbe hat…?” as a fixed chunk.

quick_check.q: “The shirt is white” — does “weiß” need an ending here?
quick_check.a: No — predicative adjectives after sein never change

topics.summary: Ordering food, shopping for groceries, and talking about meals ties together everything you’ve learned so far — nouns and gender, accusative case, modal verbs (möchten), and numbers all come together in one of the most common real-life conversations you’ll have.

levels.name: Elementary
levels.desc: You start combining ideas: the past tense, the dative case, comparisons, reflexive verbs, and your first subordinate clauses.

topics.summary: The dative case marks the indirect object — the person or thing that something is given, said, or shown to. It changes all three articles (unlike the accusative, which only changed “der”), and it’s required after a fixed set of common prepositions.

cards.desc: Ich gebe dem Kunden die Rechnung. — I give the customer (dative) the invoice (accusative).
Masculine/neuter: der/das → dem. Feminine: die → der. Plural: die → den (+n on the noun!).
Some verbs take a dative object with NO accusative at all: Ich helfe dir. Das gefällt mir.

cards.en: aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu
cards.desc: These 7 prepositions are ALWAYS followed by the dative, with no exceptions — worth memorising as a chant.

topics.rule_note: In the dative plural, the noun itself also gets an -n if it doesn’t already end in one: die Kinder → den Kindern; die Autos → den Autos (already ends in -s, no change).

rules_table.title: Article Endings Across All Three Cases So Far
rules_table.sub: Compare nominative, accusative, dative side by side

example_main.de: Ich danke dir und helfe gern meinen Kollegen.
example_main.en: I thank you and I’m happy to help my colleagues.

extra_examples.de: Das Geschenk gehört meiner Schwester.

topics.tip: Memorise the 7 dative-only prepositions as one chant: aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu (“out of, at/near, with, after/to, since, from, to”). Say it daily until it’s automatic.
topics.warning: “mit dem Bus”, not “mit den Bus” — mit always forces dative, even though “der Bus” is masculine and your accusative instinct (Unit 6, A1) might want to say “den”.

quick_check.q: Name three of the 7 fixed dative prepositions
quick_check.a: any of: aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu

topics.summary: Nine common prepositions can take EITHER the accusative or the dative, depending on whether they describe movement toward a place (accusative) or a fixed location / movement within a place (dative). This single distinction — “wohin?” vs. “wo?” — is one of the most useful grammar rules in the whole language.

cards.desc: Ich gehe in die Küche. (I’m going INTO the kitchen — crossing into a new location.)
Ich bin in der Küche. (I AM in the kitchen — static location, no movement between places.)

cards.en: an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen
cards.desc: at/on, on/upon, behind, in, next to, over/about, under, in front of, between.
“Wohin legst du das Buch?” (accusative answer) vs. “Wo liegt das Buch?” (dative answer).

topics.rule_note: Some verbs are also “two-way” themselves: stellen/legen/setzen (to place, upright/flat/sitting) always take the accusative (an action of placing), while stehen/liegen/sitzen (to stand/lie/sit) always take the dative (a state of being).

rules_table.title: Accusative vs. Dative in Action
rows: Ich hänge das Bild an die Wand.
movement — the picture is going ONTO the wall
Das Bild hängt an der Wand.
location — the picture is already there
Wir setzen uns auf das Sofa.
movement — sitting down = a change of state

example_main.de: Ich stelle den Laptop auf den Tisch, dann steht er auf dem Tisch.
example_main.en: I place the laptop on the table, then it stands on the table.

extra_examples.de: Gehst du heute Abend ins Kino?
extra_examples.en: Are you going to the cinema tonight? (in + das = ins)

extra_examples.de: Das Kino ist im Stadtzentrum.

topics.tip: Two contractions appear constantly: in + das = ins and in + dem = im. Learn them as fixed words — „Ich gehe ins Büro“ and „Ich bin im Büro“ are both extremely common.
topics.warning: Don’t assume all 9 prepositions are “usually” one case — the case depends 100% on the sentence’s meaning (movement vs. location) each time, never on the preposition alone.

topics.summary: Spoken German almost always uses the Perfekt to talk about the past, not a simple past-tense verb form. It’s built from a helper verb (haben or sein) in the present tense, plus the main verb’s past participle pushed to the very end — the same “verb bracket” you saw with modals.

cards.desc: Ich habe gearbeitet. (I worked / have worked.) The large majority of verbs take haben.
Ich bin gefahren. (I drove/went.) Used for movement (gehen, fahren, fliegen) and change of state (werden, sterben) + sein/bleiben.
machen → gemacht, lernen → gelernt. Predictable and easy once you’ve seen the pattern a few times.
sprechen → gesprochen, sehen → gesehen, gehen → gegangen — these must be memorised individually.

topics.rule_note: Verbs ending in -ieren (often borrowed from French/Latin) drop the ge- prefix entirely: studieren → studiert, telefonieren → telefoniert (not „gestudiert“).
topics.table_sub: Learn these 12 first — they cover a huge share of daily speech

example_main.de: Gestern habe ich lange gearbeitet und bin dann nach Hause gefahren.
example_main.en: Yesterday I worked for a long time and then drove home.

extra_examples.de: Hast du die E-Mail schon gelesen?
extra_examples.en: Have you already read the e-mail?

extra_examples.de: Wir haben letzte Woche einen neuen Server installiert.
extra_examples.en: We installed a new server last week.

extra_examples.de: Sie ist letztes Jahr nach Deutschland gezogen.
extra_examples.en: She moved to Germany last year.

extra_examples.de: Ich habe drei Jahre in einem Rechenzentrum gearbeitet.
extra_examples.en: I worked at a data center for three years.

topics.tip: When in doubt about haben vs. sein, ask: does the verb describe motion FROM one place TO another, or a change of state? If yes → sein. Everything else (including all reflexive verbs) → haben.
topics.warning: “Ich bin gearbeitet” is wrong — arbeiten is not a motion verb, so it always takes haben: Ich habe gearbeitet.

topics.title_en: Simple Past of sein, haben & Modals
topics.summary: While most verbs use the Perfekt (Unit 3) in speech, a handful of high-frequency verbs — sein, haben, and the modal verbs — almost always appear in their simple past (Präteritum) form instead, even in casual conversation. These forms are worth memorising as a separate set.

cards.desc: Ich war müde. (I was tired.) Ich hatte keine Zeit. (I had no time.) Used constantly, in place of the clunkier Perfekt forms.
Modal verbs almost always use Präteritum too: Ich musste arbeiten. (I had to work.)
The modal’s umlaut disappears in Präteritum: konnte, durfte, musste — all lose the umlaut they had in infinitive form.
Outside of sein/haben/modals, using Präteritum in speech can sound overly formal or literary — stick to Perfekt for regular verbs.

topics.rule_note: A simple memory trick: war and hatte are shorter and easier to say quickly than „ich bin gewesen“ or „ich habe gehabt“ — which is exactly why native speakers default to them even in relaxed conversation.
stats: Practical rule: shorter wins in speech
topics.table_sub: The set every learner should simply memorise

example_main.de: Ich hatte gestern viel zu tun und konnte dich deshalb nicht anrufen.

extra_examples.de: Wir waren letztes Jahr in Berlin.

topics.tip: You will meet full Präteritum for ALL verbs when reading news articles, books, and formal writing (B1/B2) — but for now, only sein/haben/modals need active, spoken mastery.

topics.summary: Many German verbs are built from a base verb plus a prefix. Separable prefixes detach and fly to the end of the sentence in the present tense; inseparable prefixes never detach at all. Telling them apart is mostly about where the stress falls when you say the word.

cards.desc: In the present tense the prefix jumps to the very end: Ich stehe um sechs Uhr auf. (I get up at six.)
be-, ge-, er-, ver-, zer-, ent-, emp-, miss- never separate: Ich verstehe das. (I understand that.)
Separable verbs insert -ge- between prefix and stem: aufgestanden. Inseparable verbs skip ge- entirely: verstanden.
stehen (to stand) becomes completely different verbs with prefixes: aufstehen (get up), verstehen (understand).

topics.rule_note: Quick separable-prefix list to recognise on sight: auf-, an-, ab-, aus-, ein-, mit-, vor-, zu-, zurück-, weg-. If you can imagine the prefix as its own little word, it’s separable.
stats: Where separable prefix goes: sentence end

rules_table.title: Separable vs. Inseparable — Side by Side
rows: Ich habe ein Paket bekommen. (no ge-)

example_main.de: Ich stehe früh auf, dusche, und rufe dann meine Mutter an.
example_main.en: I get up early, shower, and then call my mother.

extra_examples.de: Kommst du heute Abend mit?
extra_examples.en: Are you coming along tonight?

extra_examples.de: Wir haben das Problem endlich verstanden.
extra_examples.en: We finally understood the problem.

extra_examples.de: Ich habe ein neues Angebot bekommen.
extra_examples.en: I received a new offer.

extra_examples.de: Sie macht das Fenster zu, weil es kalt ist.

quick_check.a: at the very end of the sentence
No — inseparable prefixes never take ge-

topics.summary: In A1 (Unit 11) you met mein/dein in the nominative. Now that you know all three cases, here is the full declension — possessive articles follow EXACTLY the same ending pattern as “ein” across nominative, accusative, and dative.

cards.desc: The base forms before any case ending is added — add the same endings as “ein” gets.
euer loses its middle -e- with a vowel ending: eure Mutter (not eu<u>er</u>e).
If you know ein/einen/einem for masculine, you already know mein/meinen/meinem — identical suffixes.
Nominative/accusative feminine and all-case plural always add -e: meine Schwester, meine Eltern.

topics.rule_note: Think of possessive articles as “ein with a different front half” — the ENDING always matches what „ein“ would take in that case, gender and number. This is the single biggest shortcut in this unit.
topics.table_sub: Every other possessive follows this exact pattern

example_main.en: I explained my idea to my boss.

topics.tip: “Ihr” (capitalised) is formal “your”; “ihr” (lowercase) is “her” or “their” — only capitalisation tells them apart in writing, so context matters just as much when listening.

topics.summary: You saw in A1 that adjectives need no ending after “sein”. But an adjective placed directly BEFORE a noun always takes an ending that shows the noun’s case, gender and number. This unit covers the pattern after der/die/das words — the full three-way system arrives in B1.

cards.desc: der große Tisch, die große Lampe, das große Fenster — nominative singular always ends in -e.
The only change from nominative in this pattern: masculine accusative switches -e to -en.

cards.en: die großen Tische, dem großen Tisch
cards.desc: Once you’re not in the nominative/masc.-accusative slot, the ending is reliably -en almost everywhere.

cards.de: The article already shows the case
cards.desc: Because der/die/das already signals case and gender, the adjective’s job is smaller here — hence “weak declension”.

topics.rule_note: Memorise this shortcut: after der-words, the adjective ending is -e in exactly two spots (nom. all genders, and accusative fem./neut.) and -en everywhere else.
topics.table_sub: “der große/große/große Tisch/Lampe/Fenster” pattern

example_main.de: Der neue Kollege sitzt neben dem großen Fenster.
example_main.en: The new colleague sits next to the big window.

extra_examples.de: Ich mag die moderne Architektur dieser Stadt.
extra_examples.en: I like the modern architecture of this city.

extra_examples.de: Wir haben den alten Router gegen den neuen getauscht.
extra_examples.en: We swapped the old router for the new one.

extra_examples.de: Das kleine Café an der Ecke ist sehr gemütlich.
extra_examples.en: The small café on the corner is very cosy.

extra_examples.de: Ich arbeite gern mit den freundlichen Kollegen zusammen.

topics.tip: Practice with one adjective (groß) across the whole table above until the -e/-en pattern feels automatic, THEN apply it to new adjectives — the ending logic never changes, only the adjective does.

topics.summary: Comparing things in German is refreshingly regular: add -er for “more” and am -sten for “most”, similar to English “-er/-est”. A set of short, common adjectives also add an umlaut, and a few irregular forms simply need to be memorised.

cards.desc: billig → billiger (cheaper), klein → kleiner (smaller). Used with „als“ for “than”: schneller als ich.
Used predicatively (after sein): Das ist am schnellsten. (That is the fastest.)
One-syllable words with a, o, u often gain an umlaut: groß → größer, kurz → kürzer.
gut → besser → am besten. viel → mehr → am meisten. gern → lieber → am liebsten.

topics.rule_note: For “as…as” (equal comparison), German uses genauso…wie or so…wie: „Er ist so groß wie ich.“ (He is as tall as me.) — the adjective stays in its base form here.
topics.table_sub: Regular pattern first, then the irregulars to memorise

example_main.de: Diese Lösung ist schneller als die alte, aber die dritte Option ist am besten.
example_main.en: This solution is faster than the old one, but the third option is the best.

extra_examples.de: Mein Bruder ist älter als ich, aber meine Schwester ist am jüngsten.
extra_examples.en: My brother is older than me, but my sister is the youngest.

extra_examples.de: Ich trinke lieber Tee als Kaffee.
extra_examples.en: I’d rather drink tea than coffee.

extra_examples.de: Dieses Angebot ist genauso gut wie das andere.
extra_examples.en: This offer is just as good as the other one.

extra_examples.de: Am liebsten arbeite ich am frühen Morgen.
extra_examples.en: I like working best in the early morning.

topics.tip: „am liebsten“ is one of the most useful phrases in everyday German for expressing preference — practise it with different verbs: Ich esse am liebsten Pizza. Ich reise am liebsten im Sommer.

topics.summary: Reflexive verbs describe an action the subject does to or for itself, and they need a reflexive pronoun (mich, dich, sich…) alongside the verb. Some verbs are ALWAYS reflexive in German even when the English translation has no “myself/yourself” at all.

cards.desc: Ich wasche mich. (I wash myself.) The pronoun matches the subject and is usually accusative.
Ich freue mich auf das Wochenende. (I’m looking forward to the weekend — no literal “self” in English.)
Unlike mich/dich, the 3rd person and formal “you” always use the same word: sich.

cards.de: Some verbs can take a dative reflexive
cards.desc: Ich kaufe mir ein Buch. (I’m buying myself a book.) — dative because “ein Buch” is already the accusative object.

topics.rule_note: The reflexive pronoun sits right after the conjugated verb, in the normal object position — „Ich interessiere mich für Technik.“ — exactly where any other object pronoun would go.
topics.table_sub: The pronoun set, plus common reflexive verbs to know

example_main.de: Ich freue mich sehr, dich kennenzulernen.
example_main.en: I’m very happy to meet you.

extra_examples.de: Beeil dich, der Zug fährt gleich!
extra_examples.en: Hurry up, the train is leaving soon!

extra_examples.de: Wir erinnern uns gut an unsere Reise.
extra_examples.en: We remember our trip well.

extra_examples.de: Interessierst du dich für neue Technologien?
extra_examples.en: Are you interested in new technologies?

extra_examples.de: Am Wochenende ruhe ich mich richtig aus.
extra_examples.en: On the weekend I really rest.

topics.tip: Build a personal list of “always-reflexive” verbs as you meet them — there’s no rule that predicts which verbs are reflexive in German, so like noun gender, they’re learned one at a time.

topics.summary: The imperative gives instructions, requests, and commands — essential for following recipes, workplace instructions, safety signs, and giving directions. German has three imperative forms matching du, ihr, and Sie.

cards.desc: Drop -st from the du-form and often the final -e: du kommst → Komm! (Stem-changing e→i verbs keep the change: Sprich!)
Identical to the normal ihr-conjugation, just without the pronoun: ihr kommt → Kommt!
Formal command: conjugated verb, then “Sie” — identical word order to a yes/no question, but with an exclamation mark, not a question mark.
Sei pünktlich! (Be on time! - du) Seid leise! (Be quiet! - ihr) Seien Sie so gut... (Be so kind... - Sie)

topics.rule_note: Add „bitte“ (please) to soften any command — „Kommen Sie bitte herein.“ (Please come in.) is standard, polite workplace German.
topics.table_sub: du / ihr / Sie side by side

example_main.de: Setzen Sie sich bitte, und füllen Sie dieses Formular aus.
example_main.en: Please sit down, and fill out this form.

extra_examples.de: Sei bitte pünktlich morgen!
extra_examples.en: Please be on time tomorrow!

extra_examples.de: Vergiss deinen Ausweis nicht!
extra_examples.en: Don’t forget your ID!

extra_examples.de: Schauen Sie bitte hier nach links.
extra_examples.en: Please look to the left here.

extra_examples.de: Ruft mich an, wenn ihr ankommt!
extra_examples.en: Call me when you (all) arrive!

topics.warning: A separable verb still separates in the imperative: aufstehen → Steh auf! (du), Stehen Sie auf! (Sie) — the prefix goes to the end, exactly like in a normal sentence.

topics.summary: Your first subordinate clauses — connecting two ideas with “because”, “that”, or “if/when”. The grammar payoff is significant: in a subordinate clause, the conjugated verb jumps all the way to the end of the clause, unlike in a normal main clause.

cards.desc: Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Deutschland arbeiten möchte. — the verb „möchte“ moves to the very end.
Ich weiß, dass du hart arbeitest. (I know that you work hard.) — introduces a reported idea.
Wenn ich Zeit habe, lerne ich Deutsch. (When/if I have time, I learn German.)
If the subordinate clause opens the sentence, the two verbs meet at the comma: „Wenn ich Zeit habe, lerne ich...“

topics.rule_note: This is called verb-last word order (Verbletztstellung). In English nothing moves — “because I want to work” keeps normal order — but in German the conjugated verb is always pushed to the end of a weil/dass/wenn clause. This is one of the biggest structural differences between the two languages.

rules_table.title: Main Clause vs. Subordinate Clause Word Order
rows: Ich denke, dass er heute nicht kommt.
Wenn ich Zeit habe, rufe ich dich an.

example_main.de: Ich bin spät dran, weil der Bus nicht gekommen ist.
example_main.en: I’m late because the bus didn’t come.

extra_examples.de: Ich glaube, dass diese Lösung besser ist.
extra_examples.en: I believe that this solution is better.

extra_examples.de: Wenn du Fragen hast, kannst du mich immer anrufen.
extra_examples.en: If you have questions, you can always call me.

extra_examples.de: Sie ist froh, dass sie den Job bekommen hat.
extra_examples.en: She’s glad that she got the job.

extra_examples.de: Wir bleiben zu Hause, weil es stark regnet.
extra_examples.en: We’re staying home because it’s raining hard.

topics.warning: A very common beginner mistake: „weil ich möchte lernen“ (keeping normal order). The correct form pushes BOTH the modal and its infinitive to the end, modal last: „weil ich lernen möchte“.

quick_check.q: Where does the verb go in a weil/dass/wenn clause?
quick_check.a: all the way to the end

die Umkleidekabine = the fitting room. Es passt (nicht) = it (doesn’t) fit.

pay by card only / in cash

topics.summary: Describing symptoms at a pharmacy or doctor’s office is a high-stakes practical skill. German uses the dative heavily here („mir tut… weh“), and body-part vocabulary connects directly back to the gender rules from A1.

cards.desc: Literally “the head hurts to me” — dative pronoun + body part (nominative) + tut/tun...weh.
For minor issues, Germans go to the Apotheke first for advice/medicine before seeing a doctor (der Arzt).
Ich fühle mich nicht gut. (I don’t feel well.) Ich bin erkältet. (I have a cold.)
Ich möchte einen Termin vereinbaren. (I’d like to make an appointment.) — essential phone/reception phrase.

topics.rule_note: “weh tun” takes a dative pronoun for the person and treats the body part as the grammatical subject: Mir tun die Füße weh. (My feet hurt — lit. “the feet hurt to me”.)
topics.table_sub: der/die/das given for every noun

example_main.de: Mir tut der Kopf weh, und ich glaube, ich habe Fieber.
example_main.en: My head hurts, and I think I have a fever.

extra_examples.de: Nehmen Sie diese Tablette dreimal täglich.

topics.tip: German compounds body-part + „schmerzen“ (pain) into one word constantly: Kopfschmerzen (headache), Bauchschmerzen (stomach ache), Rückenschmerzen (back pain) — a very productive pattern.

Einfach oder hin und zurück? (One-way or round trip?) Erste oder zweite Klasse? (First or second class?)

levels.name: Intermediate
levels.desc: Independent use of German: the genitive case, full adjective endings, relative clauses, passive voice, and the subjunctive for polite and hypothetical speech.
levels.goal: handle most everyday, work and travel situations, and explain your opinion with reasons

topics.summary: The genitive expresses possession — “the customer’s laptop”, “the end of the month”. It’s gradually disappearing from casual spoken German in favour of „von + dative“, but it remains essential for formal writing, business German, and a set of common fixed prepositions.

cards.desc: One-syllable nouns usually add -es; longer ones add -s: des Mannes, des Computers.
Only the article changes to der — the noun itself stays exactly as in the nominative.
In casual speech, „von + dative“ often replaces the genitive: das Auto von meinem Vater = meines Vaters Auto.
during, despite, because of, instead of — these traditionally require genitive (dative is now common in speech, but genitive is “correct” written German).

topics.rule_note: Word order flips compared to English: der Laptop des Kunden (the customer’s laptop) puts the “owner” AFTER the thing owned — opposite of English “’s”.

rules_table.title: Genitive Forms Across Genders
rules_table.sub: Article and noun ending both matter here

example_main.de: Das ist der Laptop meines Kollegen, nicht meiner.
example_main.en: That’s my colleague’s laptop, not mine.

extra_examples.de: Wegen des schlechten Wetters bleiben wir zu Hause.
extra_examples.en: Because of the bad weather, we’re staying home.

extra_examples.de: Das Ende des Monats ist immer stressig.
extra_examples.en: The end of the month is always stressful.

extra_examples.de: Trotz der hohen Kosten haben wir das Projekt gestartet.
extra_examples.en: Despite the high costs, we started the project.

extra_examples.de: Die Firma meines Vaters ist seit 1990 aktiv.
extra_examples.en: My father’s company has been active since 1990.

topics.tip: In everyday spoken German, „wegen“ and „trotz“ are increasingly used with the dative („wegen dem Wetter“) — grammatically “incorrect” but extremely common. Use genitive in writing.

quick_check.q: “The end of the month” in genitive?

topics.summary: A2 showed you the “weak” pattern after der/die/das. Now the full picture: German has THREE declension patterns depending on what (if anything) comes before the adjective — a der-word, an ein-word, or nothing at all.

cards.desc: You know this from A2 — mostly -e/-en, since the article already shows the case.
Nominative masc./neuter and accusative neuter borrow the der-word ending (since ein has no ending there); everywhere else it matches the weak pattern.
The adjective itself carries the der-word-style ending, since there’s no article to show case/gender.
Always ask first: is there a der-word, an ein-word, or no article? That answer picks the declension table to use.

topics.rule_note: The three systems converge in the dative and genitive: almost everywhere except nominative and accusative neuter/masculine, the ending is simply -en — that’s the pattern to lean on when unsure.
stats: Shared ending in most dative/genitive slots: -en

rules_table.title: Strong Declension — No Article at All
rules_table.sub: The adjective itself signals case & gender

example_main.de: Ein erfahrener Techniker mit guten Kenntnissen wird gesucht.
example_main.en: An experienced technician with good knowledge is being sought.

extra_examples.de: Frisches Obst ist gesund.
extra_examples.en: Fresh fruit is healthy.

extra_examples.de: Wir suchen einen zuverlässigen Mitarbeiter.
extra_examples.en: We’re looking for a reliable employee.

extra_examples.de: Mit großer Freude geben wir bekannt…
extra_examples.en: With great pleasure we announce… (formal opener)

extra_examples.de: Gutes Werkzeug macht die Arbeit leichter.
extra_examples.en: Good tools make the work easier.

topics.warning: Job ads and CVs use strong/mixed declension constantly — „erfahrener Netzwerktechniker“ (no article) vs. „ein erfahrener Netzwerktechniker“ (ein-word, still -er in this slot because „ein“ has no ending of its own here).

quick_check.q: What decides which of the 3 patterns to use?
quick_check.a: whether a der-word, ein-word, or no article precedes the adjective

topics.summary: Relative clauses add extra information about a noun — “the man WHO called”, “the book THAT I read”. German relative pronouns (der, die, das…) look identical to the definite articles, and the clause always pushes its verb to the end, just like weil/dass/wenn.

cards.desc: Der Kollege, der mir geholfen hat, heißt Tom. (The colleague WHO helped me is called Tom.)
Der Kollege, den ich gestern getroffen habe. (The colleague WHOM I met yesterday.)
Der Kollege, dem ich geholfen habe. (The colleague WHOM I helped / to whom I gave help.)
Der Kollege, dessen Laptop kaputt ist. (The colleague WHOSE laptop is broken.)

topics.rule_note: The relative pronoun’s gender and number match the noun it refers back to, but its case comes from its own role inside the relative clause — the two choices are independent of each other.
stats: Comma required before every relative clause
topics.table_sub: Identical to der/die/das, except dative plural & genitive

example_main.de: Das ist die Firma, bei der ich seit drei Jahren arbeite.
example_main.en: That’s the company where (lit. “at which”) I’ve worked for three years.

extra_examples.de: Der Mitarbeiter, der die Präsentation gehalten hat, ist neu.
extra_examples.en: The employee who gave the presentation is new.

extra_examples.de: Das Projekt, an dem wir arbeiten, ist fast fertig.
extra_examples.en: The project we’re working on is almost finished.

extra_examples.de: Ich kenne die Frau, deren Sohn hier studiert.
extra_examples.en: I know the woman whose son studies here.

extra_examples.de: Das sind die Kollegen, denen ich vertraue.
extra_examples.en: Those are the colleagues I trust.

topics.tip: A relative clause with a preposition puts the preposition BEFORE the pronoun, not stranded at the end like English: „the project (that) we’re working <u>on</u>“ → „das Projekt, <u>an</u> dem wir arbeiten“.

quick_check.q: What determines the relative pronoun’s CASE?
quick_check.a: its grammatical role inside the relative clause

topics.summary: Beyond weil/dass/wenn, B1 expects a wider toolkit of connectors for contrast, purpose, and time — all of which trigger the same verb-last word order you already know.

cards.desc: Obwohl es regnet, gehen wir spazieren. (Although it’s raining, we’re going for a walk.)
Ich spreche langsam, damit du mich verstehst. (I speak slowly so that YOU understand — different subject than “um…zu”, Unit 8.)
Während ich arbeite, höre ich Musik. Bevor ich gehe, räume ich auf. Nachdem ich gegessen hatte, ging ich.
Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt. (I don’t know whether he’s coming.) — „ob“ reports a yes/no question, „wenn“ is a condition.

topics.rule_note: „nachdem“ usually pairs with Plusquamperfekt (had + past participle) in the subordinate clause when the main clause is in the Perfekt/Präteritum: „Nachdem ich gegessen hatte, bin ich gegangen.“ — the eating happened before the leaving.
topics.table_sub: All trigger verb-last word order

example_main.de: Obwohl ich müde war, habe ich weitergearbeitet, damit das Projekt fertig wird.
example_main.en: Although I was tired, I kept working so that the project would be finished.

extra_examples.de: Bevor du gehst, schick mir bitte die Datei.
extra_examples.en: Before you leave, please send me the file.

extra_examples.de: Ich weiß nicht, ob wir das Ziel erreichen.
extra_examples.en: I don’t know whether we’ll reach the goal.

extra_examples.de: Während meine Kollegin telefoniert, schreibe ich die E-Mail.
extra_examples.en: While my colleague is on the phone, I’m writing the e-mail.

extra_examples.de: Nachdem er die Prüfung bestanden hatte, feierte er.
extra_examples.en: After he had passed the exam, he celebrated.

topics.warning: Don’t confuse ob (whether, reporting a yes/no question) with wenn (if/when, a condition): „Ich frage, ob er kommt“ ≠ „Ich frage, wenn er kommt“ — the second is grammatically odd.

quick_check.a: Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt

topics.summary: The passive shifts focus from WHO does an action to WHAT happens — common in instructions, news, and technical/workplace writing. It’s built with werden + past participle, and the doer (if mentioned) appears after von + dative.

cards.desc: The problem is (being) solved. — werden conjugates for tense; the participle stays at the end.

cards.en: Das Problem wird vom Techniker gelöst.
cards.desc: The problem is solved BY the technician. — „von“ introduces the (optional) agent.
Present: wird gelöst. Past (Präteritum): wurde gelöst. Perfekt: ist gelöst worden (note: geworden → worden).
Describes the RESULT/state, not the action itself: „Der Laptop ist repariert“ (it’s already fixed) vs. „wird repariert“ (it’s being fixed now).

topics.rule_note: In the Perfekt passive, the participle of werden drops its ge- prefix and becomes worden, not „geworden“ — this is a genuine exception worth memorising on its own.
topics.table_sub: “Das Formular wird/wurde/ist ausgefüllt worden”
table_rows: The form is being filled out.
The form has been filled out.
The form must be filled out.

example_main.de: Die neue Firewall wird nächste Woche vom IT-Team installiert.
example_main.en: The new firewall is being installed next week by the IT team.

extra_examples.de: Der Bericht wurde gestern fertiggestellt.
extra_examples.en: The report was finished yesterday.

extra_examples.de: Alle Mitarbeiter werden über die Änderung informiert.
extra_examples.en: All employees are being informed about the change.

extra_examples.de: Das Problem ist bereits gelöst worden.
extra_examples.en: The problem has already been solved.

extra_examples.de: Diese Regeln müssen von allen beachtet werden.
extra_examples.en: These rules must be observed by everyone.

topics.tip: Job descriptions and technical manuals lean heavily on passive voice — recognising it quickly (rather than translating word-for-word) will speed up your reading comprehension enormously.

quick_check.q: What does “worden” replace in the Perfekt passive?

topics.summary: Konjunktiv II expresses politeness, wishes, hypotheticals, and advice — the German equivalent of “would, could, should”. In daily speech it’s almost always built with würde + infinitive, except for a handful of extremely common irregular forms.

cards.desc: Ich würde gern helfen. (I would like to help.) Works for almost any verb, like English “would + verb”.
For sein, haben, and modal verbs, native speakers use the direct Konjunktiv II form instead of würde: Ich hätte gern…, Ich wäre froh…
Softens a request considerably compared to the plain present tense — the standard polite register in shops, offices, and emails.

cards.en: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich…
cards.desc: “If I had time, I would…” — both clauses shift into Konjunktiv II together.

topics.rule_note: As a rule of thumb: use the direct irregular form for sein, haben, and the modal verbs (wäre, hätte, könnte, müsste, sollte, dürfte); use würde + infinitive for everything else.
topics.table_sub: Memorise these directly; they’re used constantly
table_rows: I could / would be able to
I would like (already met in A1!)

example_main.de: Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen? Ich hätte eine Frage.
example_main.en: Could you help me please? I would have a question.

extra_examples.de: Wenn ich mehr Geld hätte, würde ich reisen.
extra_examples.en: If I had more money, I would travel.

extra_examples.de: An deiner Stelle würde ich das nicht machen.
extra_examples.en: In your place, I wouldn’t do that.

extra_examples.de: Es wäre gut, wenn wir das morgen besprechen könnten.
extra_examples.en: It would be good if we could discuss that tomorrow.

extra_examples.de: Ich würde gerne in Deutschland arbeiten.
extra_examples.en: I would like to work in Germany.

topics.tip: „Ich hätte gern…“ (Unit 15, A1) was your very first taste of Konjunktiv II, long before you knew its name — you’ve already been using this mood in fixed phrases for a while.

topics.summary: German often uses the present tense with a time word for the future („Ich fahre morgen“), but Futur I — werden + infinitive — adds emphasis, certainty, or is used for predictions and promises about the more distant future.

cards.desc: The conjugated werden takes position 2; the infinitive goes to the very end — the same bracket pattern as modals.

cards.en: Ich fahre nächstes Jahr nach Deutschland.
cards.desc: With a clear time marker, present tense alone signals the future — very common in everyday speech.
Used for assumptions, promises, and formal announcements: „Die Preise werden steigen.“ (Prices will rise.)
Adding „wohl“ (probably) to Futur I is a very common way to express a guess about the present, not just the future.

topics.rule_note: Don’t confuse the auxiliary werden (will) with the main verb werden (to become): „Er wird Arzt.“ (He is becoming a doctor.) vs. „Er wird Arzt werden.“ (He will become a doctor.)
stats: Ways to express future: present tense / Futur I
Double meaning of werden: will / to become
topics.table_sub: werden (conjugated) + main verb (infinitive, at the end)

example_main.de: Nächstes Jahr werde ich in Deutschland arbeiten.
example_main.en: Next year I will work in Germany.

extra_examples.de: Es wird wahrscheinlich regnen, nimm einen Schirm mit.
extra_examples.en: It will probably rain, take an umbrella.

extra_examples.de: Wir werden das Projekt bis Freitag fertigstellen.
extra_examples.en: We will finish the project by Friday.

extra_examples.de: Die Firma wird nächsten Monat expandieren.
extra_examples.en: The company will expand next month.

extra_examples.de: Ich werde dir morgen Bescheid geben.
extra_examples.en: I’ll let you know tomorrow.

topics.tip: For everyday plans, native speakers usually prefer present tense + time word over Futur I — reserve „werden“ for emphasis, promises, predictions, or when there’s no other time marker in the sentence.

quick_check.q: Where does the infinitive go in Futur I?
quick_check.a: at the very end of the sentence

topics.summary: Certain verbs and expressions connect to a second verb using zu + infinitive (not a conjugated verb). “Um…zu” specifically expresses purpose — “in order to” — and is only used when the subject of both actions is the same.

cards.desc: Common trigger verbs: versuchen, planen, hoffen, vergessen, beginnen — “I try/plan/hope/forget/begin TO [verb]”.

cards.en: Ich lerne Deutsch, um zu arbeiten.
cards.desc: Expresses purpose, same subject in both parts: „Ich lerne Deutsch, um in Deutschland zu arbeiten.“
If the “why” involves a DIFFERENT subject, you must use „damit“ instead: „Ich spreche langsam, damit <u>du</u> mich verstehst.“
With separable-prefix verbs, „zu“ is inserted between the prefix and the stem: aufzuhören, einzukaufen.

topics.rule_note: The zu-infinitive phrase is usually set off by a comma when it has its own elements (objects, adverbs): „Ich habe vergessen, dir die Datei zu schicken.“

rules_table.title: zu-Infinitiv vs. um...zu vs. damit
rows: Ich hoffe, dich bald zu sehen.
Ich spare, um ein Auto zu kaufen.
Ich spare, damit meine Familie ein Auto hat.

example_main.de: Ich habe beschlossen, mich intensiver auf die Prüfung vorzubereiten.
example_main.en: I’ve decided to prepare more intensively for the exam.

extra_examples.de: Vergiss nicht, die Tür abzuschließen.
extra_examples.en: Don’t forget to lock the door.

extra_examples.de: Wir planen, nächstes Jahr umzuziehen.
extra_examples.en: We’re planning to move next year.

extra_examples.de: Er ruft an, um den Termin zu bestätigen.
extra_examples.en: He’s calling to confirm the appointment.

extra_examples.de: Es ist wichtig, jeden Tag zu üben.
extra_examples.en: It’s important to practise every day.

topics.tip: „Es ist wichtig/notwendig/schön …, zu…“ is an extremely productive pattern for opinions and advice — „Es ist wichtig, Deutsch zu lernen.“ works as a template for dozens of statements.

quick_check.q: “I’m learning German in order to work here” (same subject)?
quick_check.a: Ich lerne Deutsch, um hier zu arbeiten

quick_check.q: When must you use „damit“ instead of „um...zu“?
quick_check.a: when the two clauses have different subjects

topics.summary: Many German verbs pair permanently with a specific preposition and case — similar to English “wait FOR” or “depend ON”, but the German pairing is often completely different from its English equivalent. These must be memorised verb-by-verb, as a set phrase.

cards.desc: Ich warte auf den Bus. (I’m waiting for the bus.) — „auf“ here, not the expected „for = für“.

cards.en: to look forward to / be happy about
cards.desc: auf + Akk. = future event: sich freuen auf die Ferien. über + Akk. = something already happened: sich freuen über ein Geschenk.
Ich denke oft an dich. (I often think of you.) — not „über“ as English “about” might suggest.
Das hängt von der Situation ab. (That depends on the situation.) — separable verb + fixed preposition combined.

topics.rule_note: Always learn these as a three-part chunk: verb + preposition + case. Writing „warten auf (+Akk.)“ in your notes, not just „warten“, will save you from constant guessing.
topics.table_sub: Memorise the whole chunk, not just the verb

example_main.de: Ich freue mich auf das Wochenende und denke schon an den Urlaub.
example_main.en: I’m looking forward to the weekend and already thinking about the vacation.

extra_examples.de: Das Ergebnis hängt von deiner Vorbereitung ab.
extra_examples.en: The result depends on your preparation.

extra_examples.de: Wir haben lange auf die Antwort gewartet.
extra_examples.en: We waited a long time for the answer.

extra_examples.de: Er interessiert sich sehr für neue Technologien.
extra_examples.en: He’s very interested in new technologies.

extra_examples.de: Nimmst du an der Besprechung teil?
extra_examples.en: Are you taking part in the meeting?

topics.tip: Build a running personal list titled “Verb + Preposition” in your notes app and add to it every time you meet a new one — this is genuinely one of the highest-value vocabulary habits at B1.

topics.summary: You’ve absorbed verb-second and verb-last rules piece by piece. Now let’s zoom out: German word order follows a small number of consistent principles across main clauses, questions, and subordinate clauses — seeing them together makes each piece click into place.

cards.desc: “Verb-second” means 2nd grammatical ELEMENT, not word: „Heute Abend gehe ich ins Kino.“ — „Heute Abend“ is one element.
When several adverbials appear together, the usual order is Temporal → Kausal → Modal → Lokal: „Ich fahre <u>morgen</u> <u>wegen der Arbeit</u> <u>schnell</u> <u>nach Berlin</u>.“
A pronoun object jumps in front of a noun object: „Ich gebe <u>es</u> meinem Kollegen“, but „Ich gebe <u>es ihm</u>.“

cards.de: Subordinate clause = 1 verb block at the end
cards.desc: weil/dass/wenn/obwohl/relative clauses all push the FULL verb complex to the very end, in reverse order if there are two verbs.

topics.rule_note: “Verb-second” is really the defining rule of German main clauses: whatever comes first (subject, time word, object, or a whole clause), the conjugated verb is always the very next element — everything else reorganises around that fixed anchor.
stats: Universal rule: verb-second in main clauses

rules_table.title: Word Order Cheat-Sheet
rows: ..., weil ich morgen nach Berlin fahre.

topics.summary: Workplace German for job applications, meetings, and everyday office life — directly relevant vocabulary for anyone building a career in a German-speaking company.

cards.desc: die Bewerbung (application), der Lebenslauf (CV/résumé), das Anschreiben (cover letter), das Vorstellungsgespräch (job interview).
der Arbeitsvertrag (employment contract), die Probezeit (probation period), die Kündigungsfrist (notice period), das Gehalt (salary).
die Besprechung/das Meeting, der Vorgesetzte (supervisor), die Abteilung (department), die Frist (deadline).
Ich möchte etwas vorschlagen. (I’d like to propose something.) Ich bin damit einverstanden. (I agree with that.)

topics.rule_note: “Ich hätte einen Vorschlag” and „Dürfte ich kurz etwas ergänzen?“ both use Konjunktiv II (Unit 6) — workplace German leans heavily on this polite register in meetings and emails.

topics.tip: German job applications traditionally include a photo and are very formally structured — research current norms for your industry, since practices are shifting, especially at international firms.

topics.summary: B1 is the level where you start engaging with news and forming opinions in German — essential for the speaking and writing parts of the B1 exam, and for genuine integration into public discourse.

cards.desc: die Nachrichten (the news), der Artikel (article), die Meldung (report/bulletin), die Quelle (source).
Meiner Meinung nach… (In my opinion…) Ich finde, dass… (I think that…) Ich bin der Ansicht, dass… (I’m of the view that…)

cards.en: Ich stimme zu / Ich bin anderer Meinung
cards.desc: Da stimme ich zu. (I agree with that.) Ich sehe das anders. (I see it differently.)
einerseits…andererseits (on one hand…on the other hand) is the standard structure for balanced opinions in B1 writing tasks.

topics.rule_note: „Ich finde, dass…“ and „Ich bin der Meinung, dass…“ both trigger a dass-clause (Unit 11, A2) — remember to push the verb to the end: „Ich finde, dass diese Lösung besser ist.“

topics.summary: You’ve now met both past tenses (Units 3 & 4, A2). B1 is the point to consolidate: when do native speakers actually choose one over the other, and how does this shift between speech and writing?

cards.desc: In spoken conversation, almost every verb (except sein/haben/modals) uses Perfekt, regardless of how long ago the event was.
Narrative writing — news articles, novels, formal reports — almost always uses Präteritum for a smoother, more literary flow.
This exception (from A2, Unit 4) holds everywhere: war, hatte, konnte, etc. are preferred in speech AND writing.
Southern Germany, Austria, and Switzerland use Perfekt even more heavily in speech; Präteritum can sound almost formal there.

topics.rule_note: Both tenses describe the same completed past action — there is no meaning difference between „Ich habe gegessen“ and „Ich aß“. The choice is about REGISTER (spoken vs. written), not about a different shade of meaning, unlike English “simple past” vs. “present perfect”.
stats: Meaning difference between the two tenses
Skill needed: recognise both, actively use Perfekt

topics.summary: Konjunktiv I is used almost exclusively for reported speech — relaying what someone else said without directly quoting them. It’s the grammar of journalism and formal reporting, and it signals “I’m repeating this, not necessarily vouching for it”.

cards.en: „Ich bin müde“ → Er sagt, er sei müde.
cards.desc: The direct quote „Ich bin müde“ becomes indirect: Er sagt, er sei müde. — sei is Konjunktiv I of sein.

cards.en: er sage, er habe, er könne
cards.desc: Present-tense-like endings, but from a slightly different base — most visible in the 3rd person singular, which is what you’ll use 90% of the time.

cards.en: Der Minister sagte, die Reform komme bald.
cards.desc: German newspapers use Konjunktiv I constantly to report statements without claiming they’re true — a built-in “according to” marker.

cards.de: Falls back to Konjunktiv II when identical
cards.en: sie sagen → sie sagten (K.I looks like indicative)
cards.desc: When Konjunktiv I is identical to the normal present tense (common in plural forms), speakers/writers switch to Konjunktiv II to keep the “reported” signal clear.

topics.rule_note: You don’t need to actively produce every Konjunktiv I form — but you DO need to recognise it instantly while reading news, official statements, or formal reports, where it appears constantly without ever being labelled as “special”.

topics.title_en: Passive with Modals & the “sein + zu” Alternative
topics.summary: B1 covered the basic passive. B2 adds two refinements: combining passive with modal verbs (“must be done”), and a compact alternative construction — sein + zu + Infinitiv — that expresses necessity or possibility without “werden” or “können/müssen” at all.

cards.desc: Das Formular muss ausgefüllt werden. (The form must be filled out.) — the modal conjugates, everything else sits at the end.
A compact, formal alternative: „ist auszufüllen“ = „muss ausgefüllt werden“ (must be filled out).
„Das Problem ist zu lösen“ can mean “must be solved” OR “can be solved” — usually clear from surrounding context, leaning toward necessity by default.
Contracts, manuals, and official forms favour „sein + zu“ for its compact, impersonal tone — recognise it fluently when reading official German.

topics.rule_note: „sein + zu + Infinitiv“ is a hallmark of formal written German — you’ll see it constantly on forms and in contracts („Die Gebühr ist bis zum 1. des Monats zu zahlen.“ — The fee is to be paid by the 1st of the month), even if you rarely produce it yourself in speech.

rules_table.title: Three Ways to Say the Same Thing
rules_table.sub: Active, modal passive, and sein+zu compared

topics.summary: German turns verbs and adjectives into nouns extremely readily — a hallmark of formal, academic and bureaucratic style. Recognising and producing nominalizations is key to sounding professional in writing, and essential for reading official texts fluently.

cards.desc: Any infinitive can become a neuter noun: lernen → das Lernen (learning, the act of). Ohne Fleiss ist das Lernen schwer.
sicher → die Sicherheit (safety), schwierig → die Schwierigkeit (difficulty), frei → die Freiheit (freedom).
lösen → die Lösung (solution), planen → die Planung (planning), prüfen → die Prüfung (exam/check).

cards.en: „weil sie sich entschieden hat“ → „durch ihre Entscheidung“
cards.desc: Formal style often condenses a full subordinate clause into a nominalized phrase + preposition — shorter and more “official” sounding.

topics.rule_note: Nominalized infinitives are always neuter (das) and always capitalised, exactly like any other noun — „das Rauchen“ (smoking), „das Lesen“ (reading), no exceptions.
stats: Gender rule: always neuter for infinitives

topics.summary: A very German feature of formal writing: instead of a relative clause, a whole descriptive phrase is packed BEFORE the noun, built around a participle. It’s compact, common in news and academic writing, and worth being able to unpack when reading — even before you try producing it yourself.

cards.en: der Mitarbeiter, der gestern eingestellt wurde
cards.desc: “the employee who was hired yesterday” — the version you already know from B1, Unit 3.
Same meaning, packed into one noun phrase: participle (eingestellte) + everything else squeezed BEFORE the noun.

cards.en: Find the noun and article first
cards.desc: Spot the article (der) and final noun (Mitarbeiter) — everything between them is one describing block; mentally turn it back into a relative clause.
Past participle = passive/completed meaning (eingestellt = hired). Present participle (+d) = active/ongoing meaning (wachsend = growing).

topics.rule_note: This is primarily a reading and comprehension skill at B2 — you will meet it constantly in newspapers, official reports and academic texts. Actively producing long chains of these is an advanced (C1) writing skill; for now, focus on decoding them fluently.
stats: Reading strategy: find article + noun first

topics.summary: Beyond obwohl/damit/während (B1), fluent argumentation needs a richer set of connectors for proportional relationships, results, and contrast — the connective tissue of sophisticated spoken and written German.

cards.desc: Je mehr ich übe, desto besser werde ich. (The more I practice, the better I get.) — both clause verbs go to the end, desto-clause is verb-second.
Es regnete stark, sodass wir zu Hause blieben. (It rained hard, so that/so we stayed home.) — different from damit (B1), which expresses purpose/intention.
Er verbesserte sein Deutsch, indem er täglich las. (He improved his German BY reading daily.)
These take position 1 or come after the verb, but do NOT push the verb to the end — they connect two MAIN clauses, unlike obwohl.

topics.rule_note: Distinguish obwohl (subordinating: „Obwohl es regnete, ...“, verb-last) from trotzdem (a connecting adverb: „Es regnete. Trotzdem sind wir gegangen.“, verb-second) — both mean “although/nevertheless” but behave completely differently grammatically.

example_main.de: Je früher wir anfangen, desto schneller sind wir fertig.
example_main.en: The earlier we start, the faster we’ll be finished.

extra_examples.de: Das Meeting dauerte länger, sodass wir den Zug verpassten.

extra_examples.de: Die Idee ist gut, allerdings fehlt uns das Budget.

topics.warning: Don’t treat „trotzdem“ like „obwohl“ grammatically — „Es regnete, trotzdem wir gingen“ is wrong. Correct: „Es regnete, trotzdem gingen wir.“ (verb-second, like any main clause).

quick_check.q: Does „trotzdem“ push the verb to the end?
quick_check.a: No — it’s verb-second, like a normal main clause

topics.summary: Futur II expresses that something will have been completed by a certain point in the future — or, just as commonly in everyday German, that you’re making an educated GUESS about something that already happened.

cards.en: Bis Freitag werde ich es erledigt haben.
cards.desc: By Friday I will have finished it. — the full “verb bracket” now has three parts stacked at the end.

cards.de: Everyday use: a guess about the past
cards.en: Er wird wohl schon angekommen sein.
cards.desc: He’s probably already arrived. — far more common in speech than its “true future perfect” meaning.

cards.de: haben or sein, same rule as Perfekt
cards.desc: Uses the same helper-verb choice as the Perfekt tense: motion/change-of-state verbs use sein, most others use haben.
The strict “will have done by then” meaning is mostly reserved for planning documents and formal writing.

topics.rule_note: In casual conversation, Futur II almost always signals a confident guess about the past, not a literal future deadline: „Sie wird wohl schon gegessen haben.“ (She’s probably already eaten.) is far more natural than using it as a strict “future perfect”.
stats: Uses: true future-perfect / guess about the past

topics.summary: Beyond wegen/trotz/während (B1), formal and written German uses a wider set of genitive prepositions — recognising and correctly using them signals a more educated, precise writing register, especially valuable in business and official communication.

cards.desc: Slightly more formal than „wegen“, very common in official announcements and reports.
Used when framing a decision or reaction as a response to a situation: Angesichts der Lage haben wir entschieden…

topics.summary: Beyond the der/die/das relative pronouns from B1, three special relative words — wo, was, and wessen — handle places, whole-clause references, and questions of possession with extra precision.

cards.en: die Stadt, wo/in der ich wohne
cards.desc: „wo“ can informally replace „in der“ for places: die Stadt, wo ich wohne = die Stadt, in der ich wohne.

cards.de: was — referring to a whole clause or “alles/nichts/etwas”
cards.en: Das ist das Beste, was ich je gegessen habe.
cards.desc: Used after alles, nichts, etwas, or when referring back to an entire previous clause, not a specific noun.
The interrogative counterpart to „dessen/deren“ (B1) — used to directly ASK about possession.
With „was“, prepositions fuse into one word: „Das, worauf ich mich freue...“ (What I’m looking forward to...) not „auf was“.

topics.rule_note: Use was instead of der/die/das when the antecedent is alles, nichts, etwas, vieles, a superlative (das Beste, was…), or an entire preceding clause rather than one specific noun.

topics.summary: B2 fluency includes knowing WHEN to shift register — the vocabulary, sentence structure, and even grammar choices differ noticeably between a text message to a friend and an email to a client. This unit maps the key markers of each register.

cards.en: „Ich habe es nicht“ not „Ich hab’s nicht“
cards.desc: Formal writing avoids spoken-style contractions (hab’s, geht’s) and slang entirely.
Official communication favors passive voice (B1/B2) and nominalization (Unit 3) over direct commands.
Formal: „Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren“ … „Mit freundlichen Grüßen“. Informal: „Hallo/Liebe(r)…“ … „Viele Grüße / LG“.
Untranslatable flavor-words (Komm mal her! Das ist halt so.) are a hallmark of natural SPOKEN, informal German — rare in formal writing.

topics.rule_note: The single biggest, most reliable marker of register is Sie vs. du (A1, Unit 2) — but true fluency also means adjusting vocabulary, sentence length, and structure together, not just the pronoun.

topics.summary: Structuring a persuasive argument, conceding a point gracefully, and building a case across several sentences — the language you need for B2 exam speaking/writing tasks and genuine workplace debate.

cards.desc: Erstens… (firstly), zweitens… (secondly), außerdem/darüber hinaus… (furthermore/moreover), schließlich… (finally).
Zwar hat er recht, aber die Situation ist komplizierter. (True, he’s right, but the situation is more complicated.) — „zwar“ triggers inverted word order.
Es steht außer Frage, dass… (There’s no question that…) Es lässt sich nicht leugnen, dass… (It cannot be denied that…)
Es scheint, dass… (It seems that…) Vermutlich/Wahrscheinlich… (Presumably/probably…) — softening certainty appropriately.

topics.rule_note: „Zwar…, aber…“ is a classic B2 structure: zwar takes position 1, forcing the verb into position 2 right after it („Zwar hat er recht,…“) — a small but very natural-sounding inversion.

topics.summary: Words that look like English cognates but mean something different — “false friends” — trip up even advanced learners. This unit collects the highest-risk ones for English speakers specifically.

cards.desc: „Ich bekomme ein Geschenk“ = I RECEIVE a gift. “To become” is werden: „Ich werde Müde.“
A famous trap — „Gift“ means poison. “Gift” (present) is das Geschenk.
„Ich komme eventuell.“ = I might come. “Eventually” is schließlich/letztendlich.
“Sensible” (reasonable) is vernünftig. „Sensibel“ describes emotional sensitivity, closer to English “sensitive”.

topics.rule_note: When a German word looks suspiciously similar to an English one, treat that as a yellow flag, not confirmation — verify the meaning before using it, especially in professional writing where a false friend can genuinely confuse your reader.
stats: Rule of thumb: verify, don’t assume
